class_id: a value passed to a resolver so it can JUDGE is treated by that resolver as a value being ASSERTED
feature: any conflict resolver, merge step, consolidator or reconciler whose input is one flat object, where the caller must supply both (a) the values it is actually claiming and (b) surrounding facts the resolver needs in order to judge those claims
symptom: the resolver needs context to do its job — an entity's type to pick validation thresholds, a segment to choose plausibility floors, a status to decide which rules apply. The caller has that context sitting on the stored row, so it reads it from there and puts it in the same payload as the real claims, because the payload is one flat object and there is nowhere else to put it. The resolver cannot tell the two apart: every key it receives is a claim by the caller's source. The context values are usually IDENTICAL to what is stored (they came from there), so nothing visibly changes and no test fails — but provenance is re-stamped to the caller's source, and any convergence logic reads 'both sides now agree' and CLOSES open disagreements about fields the caller never examined. The damage is invisible precisely because the numbers do not move: the audit trail changes while the data does not. The generic test is to ask, of every key in a resolver's input, 'is the caller ASSERTING this, or does the caller merely NEED it?' — and to check whether the resolver has any way to be told which is which.
first_seen: 2026-09-21 — IPODhan, the offer-document write path, found by tracing the owner's rule 'a new document should only be adjudicated on its own fields'. `filing-persister.ts:1228-1242` builds its payload by reading five identity fields off the EXISTING row (`companyName`, `segment`, `offeringType`, `status`, `listingExchange`), plus `openDate`/`closeDate` fallbacks at 1289-1303. They are needed as context — the consolidator reads `segment` and `offeringType` to choose validation thresholds (an SME issue has different plausibility floors than a mainboard one). But the consolidator iterates `Object.keys(incomingData)` (`data-consolidation-service.ts:1068-1073`) and treats every key as a claim by source `DRHP`. Fields the document genuinely did not supply arrive `undefined` and ARE correctly skipped (guard at 1427-1444, `NO_INCOMING_VALUE`, no conflict row) — so the system already obeys the rule for the ordinary case. The re-asserted five are not undefined, pass the guard, enter full resolution, and on an equal value hit `autoResolveConverged` (1903-1912), closing open conflicts for fields the document never read. MEASURED EXPOSURE, and it is much smaller than the field counts suggest: of 31,755 auto-resolved conflicts on staging, only **23** involve `DRHP` on either side at all, and only **11** are on the re-asserted fields (9 `companyName`, 2 `status`). A first count of 18,583 'suspect' rows was wrong — it counted every auto-resolution on those FIELD NAMES, but the top pairs are website-vs-website (NSE/MONEYCONTROL 3,209 on `openDate`, BSE/CHITTORGARH 2,394 on `companyName`), which are genuine convergence between two real sources and nothing to do with this path.
fix_prs: not yet built; owner approved the approach 2026-09-21. Separate the two roles rather than trying to guess them apart inside the resolver: (1) pass the identity fields as an explicit CONTEXT parameter the resolver may read but never treats as a claim; (2) restrict resolution to the fields the document actually extracted, using the `onlyFields` narrowing that already exists at `data-consolidation-orchestrator.ts:281-286` and which this path simply does not use; (3) refuse `autoResolveConverged` for any field absent from the incoming document — closing a conflict is a claim about evidence, and re-sending a stored value is not evidence. Recorded as owner decision OD-66.
detection_check: none built. The runtime check that would have caught it: assert that every field a write path resolves is a field that write path's EXTRACTOR actually returned, and alert on the difference — the set subtraction is cheap and the answer should always be empty. A conflict-level variant, narrower and also cheap: never allow an auto-resolution whose two sides are the same underlying source (here both were effectively the stored row, arriving once as `existing` and once as a re-asserted `DRHP` claim). Note what made the exposure measurable at all: `data_conflicts` stores BOTH source names per row, so 'which resolutions involved a document' was one query. A conflict table recording only the winner could not have been decomposed this way, and the 11 real rows would have stayed hidden inside 18,583 innocent ones.
